title: North and South: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Industrial Landscape and Moral Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked — a close reading of Elizabeth Gaskell's great novel of industrial England, moral conflict, and unlikely love.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through the novel passage by passage — with three brilliant companions who will not always agree.
That disagreement, I should say upfront, is not a problem to be managed — it is the whole point.
Let me introduce them.
Oliver Trevelyan has given his voice to more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears Gaskell the way a musician hears a score, feeling where the rhythm wants to breathe.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose instinct is always toward character and moral imagination — he is suspicious, he will tell you himself, of readings that treat novels as pamphlets.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in a novel as a mechanism of power — and who will show us, I think, that Gaskell was more radical than she knew.
We begin today with three passages that span the full moral geography of the novel — labour betrayal, pastoral elegy, and an act of extraordinary financial courage.
Daniel, you have all three of today's passages — and what a range they represent.
They do represent an extraordinary range — and yet I think they speak to a single underlying question that Gaskell never stops asking.
That question is: what does loyalty cost, and who is made to bear the price?
The first passage — Higgins describing Boucher's betrayal of the Union — is one of the most morally compressed scenes in the novel.
Higgins is not a sentimental man, and his dialect carries a weight of working-class grievance that Gaskell renders with forensic precision.
Listen to what he says about Boucher going to Hamper's to beg for work:

"He went wi' his mealy-mouthed face, that turns me sick to look at, a-asking for work, though he knowed well enough the new rule, o' pledging themselves to give nought to th' Unions; nought to help the starving turn-out!"
That phrase — mealy-mouthed — is doing enormous work.
It's not simply cowardice Higgins is condemning — it's the particular dishonesty of the man who smiles while he betrays.
And then Higgins delivers the verdict — Judas.
That single biblical word, dropped into the thick of the dialect, lands like a stone in still water.
Gaskell knew exactly what she was doing when she put that word in Higgins's mouth.
The full sentence runs:
"There he went, ossing to promise aught, and pledge himsel' to aught—to tell a' he know'd on our proceedings, the good-for-nothing Judas!"
Ossing — groping toward, attempting — that's a dialect word that carries its own kind of contempt for the half-committed man.
And then the glorious irony that even Hamper — the mill owner, the enemy — turned Boucher away.
A man so thoroughly despised that even his intended master won't have him.
I want to resist, for a moment, the purely sociological reading of Boucher.
What Gaskell is also examining here is weakness of will — a failure of individual moral fibre that is not reducible to class position.
Boucher is a man who has accepted the Union's charity and then sought to profit by abandoning its principles.
Higgins himself recognises this — note that his condemnation is moral, not merely tactical.
He says the man would have, in his own words, "clemmed to death" without the Union's help.
"Why he'd a clemmed to death, if th' Union had na helped him in his pinch."
That is gratitude betrayed — and betrayal of gratitude is among the oldest and most serious moral failings any civilisation has named.
Edmund is right that Gaskell frames this morally — but the moral frame itself is produced by material conditions.
Boucher doesn't betray the Union because he is a bad man — he betrays it because his children are starving.
The system creates the desperation that makes betrayal thinkable — and then condemns the individual for the choice the system forced.
Which brings me to the second passage — Margaret at Helstone, watching the light change through windows where trees have been cut down.
It seems on its surface to be pure pastoral elegy — but even here, the forces of change are not natural, they are imposed.
Gaskell writes:

"places were changed—a tree gone here, a bough there, bringing in a long ray of light where no light was before—a road was trimmed and narrowed, and the green straggling pathway by its side enclosed and cultivated."
A great improvement it was called — Gaskell's irony is dry but it is unmistakable.
That parenthetical — a great improvement it was called — is one of those lines you have to read twice before you hear the blade in it.
On the page it looks like neutral description — read aloud, the irony sharpens into something close to grief.
But then Gaskell does something quite extraordinary — she lifts the whole passage from the particular into the universal.
The image she reaches for:

"the natural mutations brought by days and months and years, which carry us on imperceptibly from childhood to youth, and thence through manhood to age, whence we drop like fruit, fully ripe, into the quiet mother earth."
We drop like fruit, fully ripe — that is not consolation, quite.
It is something older and stranger — acceptance without self-pity.
It is perhaps the finest piece of prose in the novel — and it earns its beauty because Margaret is not indulging in sentiment.
She is genuinely tired, genuinely bereaved by the passage of time, and Gaskell refuses to let her — or us — look away.
The novel is about many things — industrial capitalism, class, the North and the South — but at its deepest it is about learning to bear loss without bitterness.
Margaret sitting by that window, with Mr. Bell sleeping in the chair — that image is one of the quietest and most truthful in Victorian fiction.
And then we come to the third passage — and what a turn it takes.
Margaret is proposing to lend Thornton nearly two thousand pounds from her own savings — to keep Marlborough Mills running.
She frames it, pointedly, as a business arrangement advantageous to herself — and that framing is doing crucial work.
Her exact words:

"if you would take some money of mine, eighteen hundred and fifty-seven pounds, lying just at this moment unused in the bank, and bringing me in only two and a half per cent.—you could pay me much better interest, and might go on working Marlborough Mills."
She is a woman of independent means proposing to invest in industrial production — in 1855, that is almost unprecedented for a woman of her station.
The trembling in her hands as she searches for the papers — Gaskell notes that — tells us that beneath the businesslike composure she is terrified.
Terrified and magnificent — those two things at once, which is Gaskell's favourite combination for her heroines.
And notice what stops the scene cold — Thornton speaks her name.
Gaskell writes: "her very heart-pulse was arrested by the tone in which Mr. Thornton spoke."
Heart-pulse arrested — that is a physiological response rendered in almost clinical language, which makes it all the more devastating.
After all the talk of interest rates and bank percentages — the body simply stops.
That moment is, for me, the novel's emotional climax in miniature — and it works precisely because Gaskell has held everything back for so long.
The voice is described as hoarse — hoarse with feeling long suppressed — and trembling with what she calls tender passion.
Two people of considerable pride, meeting across a table covered in financial documents — and love breaking through anyway.
There is something very English about that — and something Gaskell understood better than almost any novelist of her century.
Betrayal in the mill-yards, elegy among the Helstone trees, and passion breaking through a ledger sheet — we have only just begun.
In our next segment, we'll turn to questions of industrial power and the characters who embody it — with all three of our guests in close conversation.

segments.title: Margaret's Inner Life: How a Woman Learns to See

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're turning our attention to one of the novel's most quietly extraordinary achievements — Margaret Hale's developing consciousness.
How does a young woman raised in the soft green South learn to read a hard industrial world — and herself?
Joining me are three outstanding guides to the novel.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — brings his performer's ear for the rhythms and comedy of Gaskell's prose.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, lifelong reader of novels as moral and spiritual tests of character — is here to keep us honest about what kind of story this actually is.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian and fierce reader of the class structures that novels both illuminate and obscure — will ensure we never forget the world pressing in on Margaret from outside.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — because there's a scene early in the novel where Margaret revises her first impression of Thornton, and it's almost comically self-aware.
Yes — and one must resist the temptation to rush past it, because it rewards close reading enormously.
Margaret has just met Thornton and found him rather plain and ungentlemanly — or so she thought.
Then she catches herself, and corrects the judgment with admirable precision.
Gaskell gives her this speech to her mother — and it's remarkable for what it concedes and what it withholds.
She grants him power — but frames it as something to be wary of, not admired.
And that word 'tradesman' — delivered with the most exquisite condescension — tells us everything about where Margaret stands at this moment.
She is being educated, but she doesn't yet know it.
Edmund, you've put your finger on something I find absolutely delicious about this passage.
When you read it aloud — and I've read Gaskell aloud a great deal — the comedy is right there in the rhythm.
'Sagacious, and strong, as becomes a great tradesman' — that comma before 'sagacious' is doing enormous work.
It's the pause of someone who has just talked themselves into a compliment and can barely believe they're delivering it.
Gaskell is gently, mercilessly funny about her heroine here.
And the great novelists always are — they love their protagonists too much to spare them embarrassment.
I think the comedy is real — but I'd ask what's underneath it.
Margaret reaches for the word 'tradesman' as a category that explains and contains Thornton — keeps him at a safe social distance.
What she's encountering, for the first time in her sheltered life, is industrial capital embodied in a man.
She senses the power, she respects it almost against her will, and then she reaches for a label that reassures her it belongs somewhere below her on the social ladder.
That is the beginning of her education — but Gaskell is honest enough to show us the resistance before the growth.
Daniel, I'd accept the diagnosis while resisting the vocabulary.
What Margaret is encountering is not a force of capital — it is a man of will.
And the interesting thing about a novel about character is that will — whether in a cotton manufacturer or in Margaret herself — is always the engine.
She recognises something in Thornton that corresponds to something nascent in herself.
That is why the word 'inflexible' is so charged — she is also inflexible, and hasn't quite noticed yet.
And Gaskell gives us an extraordinary counterpoint to that scene in Chapter Ten — when Margaret actually sits in the same room as Thornton and observes him with this extraordinary novelist's eye.
Oliver — you've spent a lot of time with the physicality of Gaskell's characters.
Oh, this passage is a gift — a complete gift to any reader or performer.
Margaret catches the contrast between her father and Thornton — one soft, waving, almost feminine in feature; the other all hard lines and compressed intention.
And listen to how Gaskell describes Thornton's eyes — this is the moment:
'Penetrate into the very heart and core' — that is a writer who knows exactly what she's doing.
She's writing about a man looking at a room — and she makes you feel it's an act of possession.
And then — just when you've taken in all that severity — she mentions the smile.
'The rare bright smile — like sudden sunlight' — and Margaret likes it.
That is the first crack in the wall, right there.
There's something I want to add to that — because the same chapter gives us a passage about Margaret serving tea, and it deserves the same attention.
Thornton watches Margaret — obsessively, almost — while she moves around the tea table.
Gaskell gives us the bracelet sliding down her wrist, again and again, and his helpless fascination with it.
But then she turns it, and gives us this:
'The proud air of an unwilling slave' — Gaskell uses the word 'slave' deliberately, I'd argue.
Margaret is performing domestic duty under social compulsion — and the novel sees that clearly, even when Margaret herself does not.
Her education is partly about learning the limits of that domestic role — by testing it against a world where men are enslaved rather differently.
I'll grant Gaskell the word — she was precise in her diction, always.
But I think 'unwilling slave' is comic, not political — it's Margaret's own ironic sense of herself in this domestic performance.
What interests me far more is the tenderness that follows — the little finger and thumb serving as sugar-tongues, observed between father and daughter.
Thornton wants to belong to that — to that ease and warmth and unspoken love.
That is a detail of moral and emotional precision — and it teaches him something too.
The education in this novel runs both ways.
Both ways — and nowhere is that more sharply tested than when Margaret's passion for the South draws her into open confrontation with Thornton.
Daniel — this is your passage, and it's one of the great combative moments of the novel.
It is — and what makes it great is that Margaret is wrong, and she's also right, and Gaskell doesn't flatten either truth.
She defends the South with genuine passion — 'roused by the aspersion on her beloved South to a fond vehemence of defence.'
But what she says is this — and it cuts right to the bone:
'Not only sufferers but haters' — that is not the language of sentiment.
That is a young woman looking at industrial workers and naming what she actually sees — a sullen sense of injustice — before she has any framework to explain it.
Her instinct outruns her ideology.
That's precisely how a genuinely radical novelist operates — she puts the evidence in the character's mouth before the character understands its implications.
And she ends the speech by collapsing into silence — 'angry with herself for having said so much.'
That is perfect comic — or rather tragicomic — deflation.
She's made a blazing speech — and her immediate response is not satisfaction but embarrassment.
Gaskell understands that self-consciousness — that very specifically female experience of having spoken too forcefully in company and immediately wishing the floor would open.
Thornton, of course, is electrified.
What interests me is the word 'vehemence' — which Gaskell applies to Margaret more than once.
It is not a word of approval, exactly — but it is a word of energy.
Margaret's flaws — her pride, her tendency to judge quickly, her passionate partisanship — are the same qualities that will make her capable of great moral action later.
Gaskell is in the tradition of novelists — and Burke, too, I'd say — who understand that virtue must be tested, and that tested virtue requires genuine vices to overcome.
And those vices — and virtues — come to their most extreme test in the riot, and in its long aftermath.
Edmund — you have two passages from Chapter Twenty-Three, and they show Margaret in a state of very private reckoning.
These two passages, taken together, are among the finest things in the book — and one of them is only four sentences long.
Margaret has been unable to confront what happened at the riot — what she did, what was said about her — until this moment.
She says to herself: 'Now I will think of it — now I will remember it all.'
And then Gaskell gives us this image:
Four words — 'as one who sees a vision' — and Gaskell has transformed Margaret from a social comedy into something approaching the spiritual.
There is a stillness in great fiction that is harder to achieve than any action scene — and this is it.
And the breath — 'She drew a deep breath' — three words, alone in a sentence, at the end.
In performance you'd pause for a full two beats before that line and let it land.
Gaskell knew — I'm convinced she knew — exactly how this would feel read aloud.
It's the intake of breath before an act of courage.
And then — the next passage — the courage arrives.
Margaret defends herself to herself — which is the hardest audience of all.

She justifies her intervention in the riot not by social convention but by moral duty — 'fair play on each side' — and then she reaches the declaration that I think is the moral centre of her whole character:
'I walk pure before God' — not before society, not before Thornton, not before her mother.
This is Margaret's education complete — she has learned to make her own court of appeal.
I'd push on 'complete' — because the language here is fascinating in its contradictions.
She says 'I did a woman's work' — and she means it with full dignity.
But what she did — stepping between a crowd of striking workers and a mill owner — is precisely not what 'woman's work' meant to her society.
She is redefining the term even as she uses it — claiming political action as domestic virtue.
That is not the language of someone who has learned to accept her place.
That is the language of someone who has decided to rewrite it.
And what a line to deliver.
'I walk pure before God' — I've never found a way to read that line quietly.
It insists on being spoken with full weight — and Gaskell earns every syllable of that weight.
The girl who called Thornton 'a great tradesman' with barely suppressed disdain is gone.
What we have instead is someone who has looked at the world, been changed by it, and chosen — deliberately and at cost — how to act in it.
'I walk pure before God' — it really is one of those lines that rings out across the whole novel.
Margaret, we've seen, is not just a character being educated by circumstance — she is actively, sometimes painfully, learning to see.
To see Thornton, to see the North, to see herself — and to hold all three visions together without flinching.
In our next segment, we'll look at the world pressing in on Margaret from outside — the mill, the workers, and what Gaskell makes of the conflict between them.

segments.title: The Strike and the Master: Thornton's Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We're deep in the world of Milton-Northern now — a world of smoke, pride, and the clash of two Englands.
This segment turns on Thornton — the master, the manufacturer, the man — and the various forces pressing on his sense of himself.
With us, as ever, are Oliver Trevelyan, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Dr. Daniel Rosen.
I want to begin with a pair of moments that sit in rather comic parallel — Margaret describing Thornton to her mother, and Thornton describing Margaret to his.
Oliver, these two households, these two proud families — what do you make of this double portrait?
It's one of the great comic structures in the novel, and I think it's almost never remarked upon.
Margaret, in Chapter Nine, is explaining to her mother why Mr. Thornton is not quite beyond the pale.
And the condescension is breathtaking — entirely unconscious, which makes it funnier.
She says — and this is her defence of him, mind you —
"I don't suppose his education would fit him for much else."
That is a woman taking Thornton's measure from an enormous height and finding it rather sweet that he manages so well.
Now cut to Thornton, reporting back to his mother on the same encounter.
He says — with a short scornful laugh, Gaskell tells us —
"she treated me with a haughty civility which had a strong flavour of contempt in it."
He was not wrong.
What strikes me — and I think this is where Gaskell is at her shrewdest — is that both of them are correct.
Margaret is condescending. Thornton did receive contempt.
And yet Margaret's own claim, two sentences earlier, is magnificent in its own right.
She says —
"I am myself a born and bred lady through it all, even though it comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes."
That is not arrogance — or not merely arrogance.
That is the claim that character is prior to circumstance — a claim Gaskell takes seriously throughout the novel.
Thornton himself will come to embody the same conviction from the other direction.
I want to hold that thought alongside Mrs. Thornton, because I think she is the key to understanding the whole chapter.
When Thornton delivers his account of the contempt he received, she doesn't console him.
She detonates.
Listen to what she says to herself — Gaskell gives us her inner voice in full fury —
"Boy and man, he's the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don't care if I am his mother; I can see what's what, and not be blind."
That is class pride speaking — but it's also something more intimate.
Gaskell shows us, in Chapter Twelve, that Mrs. Thornton's love for her son is entirely different in character from her love for Fanny.
Fanny gets the endearments — "love," "dear" — but John gets something more sustaining.
The narrator tells us —
"her heart gave thanks for him day and night; and she walked proudly among women for his sake."
That is not sentiment. That is the deepest form of social identity Gaskell can imagine — a mother who measures herself by her son's worth.
And yet Daniel, there's a terrible irony buried in that portrait of Mrs. Thornton's pride.
Because the same chapter shows us that she winces at Fanny — at the weakness she cannot correct and will not quite acknowledge.
Gaskell describes it as "a kind of pitying tenderness" — which is one of the most devastating phrases in the novel for a mother's love.
The woman who walks proudly for her son's sake cannot walk at all for her daughter's.
Gaskell is extraordinarily honest about that, I think.
She does not sentimentalise Mrs. Thornton into a simple figure of maternal warmth.
The narrator says — with characteristic precision — that Mrs. Thornton had "an unconscious contempt for a weak character."
And Fanny, of course, is weak in precisely those points where her mother and brother are strong.
There is something almost Johnsonian about it — the conviction that virtue and strength of will are prior to all social circumstance.
I want to move us toward something that runs underneath all of this — the world these characters inhabit beyond the drawing room.
Because while the Thorntons and the Hales are measuring each other's pride, Nicholas Higgins is carrying his dying daughter upstairs.
And what he says to Margaret as she leaves — it is one of the most shattering lines in the novel.
He struggles to say it — Gaskell marks that: he struggles —
"I could wish there were a God, if it were only to ask Him to bless thee."
That is not a pious sentiment. That is a man who has no theological comfort to offer — and gives her the only thing he has left.
And when Bessy dies, her last words — reported through her sister Mary — are for Margaret and for her father.
Mary tells Margaret —
"She loved yo' dearly. Her last words were 'Give her my affectionate respects; and keep father fro' drink.'"
Two clauses, two loyalties — and Gaskell trusts the dialect to do the emotional work.
I've read those words aloud dozens of times and they never become routine.
The tenderness and the practicality sitting side by side — that is Gaskell's genius for the working-class voice.
She never makes Higgins or Bessy picturesque. She makes them exact.
And notice where that exactness places us in relation to the Thornton drama.
The pride of the Thorntons, the contempt of the Hales — all of it sits in the same novel as Bessy Higgins dying of cotton fluff in her lungs.
Gaskell does not lecture us about the juxtaposition. She simply places it before us and waits.
There's a generosity in that — and a rigour.
She lets the pride and the grief coexist without resolving them cheaply.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the strike itself — the moment when Thornton and the workers face each other across the mill yard, and Margaret steps into the space between them.

segments.title: The Wit of Milton: Gaskell's Dark Comedy

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the programme where we take Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel apart — stitch by stitch, scene by scene.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at something that often gets overlooked in discussions of this novel: Gaskell's extraordinary tonal range.
She can move from tragic devastation to exquisite comic irony within a single chapter — sometimes within a single paragraph.
To explore that range, I'm joined by three exceptional readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novel audiobooks than any living voice — he hears the prose as performance, and he is the ideal guide to how Gaskell writes for the ear.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a lifetime's close reading — he reads North and South as a story about moral character tested by the pressures of industrial England.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — he's particularly alert to what the novel reveals about the human cost of industrial capitalism.
Oliver, I want to start with you — because when we talk about Gaskell's comedy, we need someone who understands how comedy actually works on the page and in the voice.
Where do you hear the wit first in North and South?
The wit is there from the very first scenes in Milton — but it's a wit delivered with perfect composure, which is precisely what makes it devastating.
There's a small, exquisite moment when Margaret first receives Thornton at her father's house.
Thornton is struck dumb — 'his unready words would not come' — and Margaret simply fills the silence with perfect social grace.
"Mr. Thornton, I believe!"
That exclamation mark is doing extraordinary work — it's not quite a question, not quite a statement.
It's Margaret controlling the room with one phrase, while the most powerful manufacturer in Milton stands there unable to speak.
Gaskell's comedy is always social comedy — it's about who holds the power in any given room, and how often it isn't who you'd expect.
I think that's precisely right, and it points to something deeper than comedy.
What Gaskell is doing in that moment is establishing Margaret's fundamental nature — her natural authority, which has nothing to do with rank or wealth.
The comedy, as Oliver calls it, is the friction between Thornton's industrial power and Margaret's moral self-possession.
Later, Gaskell gives us the dinner party scene — and there Thornton's silent, secret inventory of Margaret is both acutely observed and, I think, rather tender.
Gaskell sets up the contrast between Fanny's restlessness and Margaret's composure with real precision.
"He saw his sister's restless way of continually arranging some part of her gown, her wandering eyes, now glancing here, now there, but without any purpose in her observation."
Fanny is drawn with that kind of affectionate satirical precision one associates with the great Augustan novelists.
She is not wicked — she is simply empty, and Gaskell never lets us forget it.
Edmund, that word 'uneasily' — when Thornton contrasts the two women — that's where the whole texture of the prose changes.
The satirical portrait of Fanny is affectionate, yes — but it's in service of something almost anguished in Thornton.
Gaskell gives us the full sweep of how he sees Margaret — the raven hair, the ivory shoulder, the motionless hands — and then:
"Mr. Thornton sighed as he took in all this with one of his sudden comprehensive glances."
And then he turns his back on her — entirely — and throws himself into conversation with her father.
That is not comedy — that is a man doing battle with himself, and Gaskell sees it with absolute clarity.
The wit and the tragedy are never far apart in this novel — they inhabit the same sentences.
I want to hold onto that word 'comprehensive' for a moment — because I think it's more loaded than it first appears.
Thornton is a man who surveys — it's what manufacturers do: they assess, quantify, direct.
But what's satirically revealing is that this comprehensive glance overwhelms him — his own instrument of mastery defeats him.
And then there's the scene that sits entirely outside the comedy — the Boucher scene — which to my mind is the moral centre of the book.
Gaskell gives Boucher a voice that is completely unlike any other in the novel — this raw, dialect-driven grief.
He is describing what the strike — what the system — has actually cost:
"Our lile Jack, who wakened me each morn wi' putting his sweet little lips to my great rough fou' face, a-seeking a smooth place to kiss,—an' he lies clemming."
That word 'clemming' — starving — is repeated throughout the passage like a drumbeat.
Gaskell does not sentimentalise Boucher — she gives him his full humanity, his rage, his tenderness, and his threat of damnation in one breath.
Daniel, when I read that passage aloud — and I have read it many times — it never gets easier.
The dialect is not picturesque — it's the vehicle for the most precise, heartbreaking tenderness in the novel.
'A-seeking a smooth place to kiss' — a child searching his father's rough face for somewhere soft enough to put his lips.
That is not reported through Margaret's sensibility — it comes directly from Boucher's mouth, in his own words.
Gaskell trusts the reader to hear what she has put on the page without editorialising over it.
That is the mark of a writer who is, in the deepest sense, an entertainer — she never blinks, and she never moralises when the scene will do it for her.
What strikes me about the Boucher passage is how far it is from polemic — and how much closer it is to elegy.
Gaskell never presents Boucher as a representative figure — a symbol of labour — but as a specific man losing a specific child.
And then — in the very same chapter — we have the scene of Mrs. Hale's bedroom, which strikes a different but equally grave note.
Gaskell's description of death's arrival is one of the most restrained and therefore most powerful in Victorian fiction.
"There lay her mother, with an unmistakeable look on her face... Death had signed her for his own, and it was clear that ere long he would return to take possession."
Death as a creditor, arriving to collect — it has the weight of legal necessity, not melodrama.
And then Mr. Hale, the man of learning, the man of refined feeling — he cannot even find the door.
His collapse into blind, groping confusion is the most honest portrait of grief the novel offers — and it is given to the weakest man in the room.
Edmund's reading of Mr. Hale is right — but I'd add that there's also something structurally significant in who does not collapse.
Margaret does not collapse — and Gaskell returns to this again and again: Margaret's composure is both admirable and, increasingly, a burden she never chose to carry.
There is a later scene — quieter in register — which I think catches Gaskell's comic and psychological genius simultaneously.
Margaret is in the room, has been in the room — and she convinces herself that Thornton simply hasn't noticed her presence.
"As if he did not feel the consciousness of her presence all over, though his eyes had never rested on her!"
That exclamation from the narrator is the most suppressed laugh in the novel — Gaskell is entirely in on the joke.
And the joke reveals the mechanism: Margaret's self-deception is her armour, and Thornton's hyper-consciousness of her is his wound.
Gaskell is not writing romantic comedy — she's writing the psychology of two people in mutual, carefully managed denial.
'He did not feel the consciousness of her presence all over' — I always want to put a long, slow pause before that 'As if.'
Because the narrator is timing it perfectly — she lets the reader share Margaret's delusion for exactly one beat, and then punctures it.
That is comic technique of the highest order — the kind you find in the very best stage comedy.
And what makes it sting is that both characters are entirely sympathetic — neither is ridiculous, both are simply human.
What I keep hearing across all of these passages is a novelist who refuses to keep her registers separate — the comic and the tragic are always in conversation.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how Gaskell uses the industrial landscape of Milton itself — not just as backdrop, but as moral argument.

segments.title: Working Men and Belonging: Higgins as Mirror

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've been following Margaret Hale as she moves from the green parishes of the South into the smoke and din of Milton.
And in this segment we turn to the question of belonging — how a stranger finds human roots in an alien place, and what that process reveals about class, kindness, and the meaning of work.
Nicholas Higgins is the character Gaskell uses as Margaret's first real bridge into the working life of Milton — and he repays close attention.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more Victorian working men aloud than perhaps anyone, and he brings a performer's ear to the rhythms of this relationship.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings his characteristic insistence that character, not class position, is the true subject of the novel.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen will ask, as ever, what the social machinery is doing underneath the tenderness.
Oliver — the first encounter between Margaret and this careworn workman is rendered almost entirely in silence. What do you make of that?
What strikes me immediately is the economy of it — Gaskell is doing something almost cinematic before cinema existed.
We begin with the street — all those men complimenting Margaret in ways that are coarse, transactional — and then this one man says something different.
Gaskell sets it up beautifully:
"You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face."
Now on the page that reads as a compliment — charming, perhaps, slightly folk-ballad.
But read it aloud and you hear the reverse — this is a man consoling himself with someone else's good fortune.
He is careworn, the text tells us — and that word 'careworn' is doing a tremendous amount of quiet labour.
What follows — that silent recognition, those chance meetings in the street — is built entirely on that one moment of mutual understanding.
Gaskell understood that friendship between people of very different stations only becomes believable if you earn it in tiny increments.
Oliver is right about the earning — and I think that is precisely where Gaskell's moral intelligence is sharpest.
This is not a programmatic encounter — Gaskell is not engineering a lesson in cross-class sympathy.
She is dramatising something far simpler and far more profound: the capacity of a good person to be genuinely moved by another.
The flowers episode in the very next passage makes this plain.
Margaret has been out gathering wild spring flowers — dog-violets, celandines — with, as Gaskell says, 'an unspoken lament in her heart for the sweet profusion of the South.'
She meets the girl, sees her looking wistfully at the flowers, and acts — not from policy but from impulse.
This is the moral instinct Gaskell believes in — not the instinct of the reformer, but of the generous soul.
I want to hold on to that word 'impulse' for a moment — because impulse is exactly how the novel keeps its politics comfortable.
The girl is not given a name yet. She is wistful. She is 'still more unhealthy' than her already careworn father.
Gaskell has painted a picture of working-class suffering so vivid that it would demand systemic explanation — and then resolves it with a handful of hedgerow flowers.
That is not nothing — the warmth is genuine — but it is also a displacement.
What the passage does brilliantly, though — and I grant Gaskell this — is show us what the limits of individual kindness are without quite admitting it.
Bessy Higgins is dying of byssinosis — fluff on the lungs from the cotton mills. Flowers are beautiful. They are not medicine.
That is hard to argue with — and yet I think the transformation described in the passage that follows is Gaskell's real argument.
After this encounter, Margaret goes home and something shifts — not in the industrial conditions of Milton, but in her relationship to the place.
Gaskell is precise about what causes it — she rules out the weather, she rules out mere time and habituation:
"It was not the long, bleak sunny days of spring, nor yet was it that time was reconciling her to the town of her habitation."
And then the answer, stripped to its bones:
"It was that in it she had found a human interest."
A human interest. Gaskell doesn't say friendship, or sympathy, or even connection — she says interest.
That word carries both intellectual curiosity and emotional investment — and that double meaning is precisely what Higgins comes to represent for Margaret.
That reading of the word 'interest' is exactly right — and it points to something Burke understood about the nature of community.
We do not love abstractions. We love particular faces, particular voices, particular careworn men who smile at us in the street.
Gaskell understands this instinctively — and it is why Higgins works as a character where a type or a spokesman would have failed utterly.
He is not Labour. He is not the Working Class. He is Nicholas Higgins — with a sick daughter, a sharp tongue, and an instinct for loyalty.
And that loyalty endures right through to the final chapters — the round-robin petition to Thornton is one of the most quietly affecting moments in the whole novel.
Yes — and the round-robin is where I find myself genuinely moved, and genuinely troubled, at the same time.
Thornton reports it to Margaret — and the phrasing is telling:
"I had a round-robin from some of my men — I suspect in Higgins' handwriting — stating their wish to work for me, if ever I was in a position to employ men again on my own behalf."
Thornton calls it 'good' — and it is good — but what these men are petitioning for is the right to sell their labour to the same master who locked them out.
Higgins's loyalty is real and it is admirable — and it is also, in structural terms, a form of submission.
What Gaskell cannot quite imagine is workers organising for power rather than petitioning for readmission.
Daniel, you are absolutely right — and Gaskell, I suspect, would have found that critique uncomfortable precisely because she couldn't refute it.
But I keep coming back to the texture of the thing — that parenthesis, 'I suspect in Higgins' handwriting.'
Thornton doesn't know for certain. He suspects. He recognises the man's voice in the pen.
That is the novel's great achievement — it has made Higgins's voice so individual, so irreducible, that even a document he may have written is recognisable as his.
And that individuality — that irreducibility, as Oliver puts it — is perhaps the hinge on which this whole discussion turns.
Higgins begins the novel as a careworn face in the street and ends it as a man whose handwriting Thornton can identify — and that is a remarkable journey.
Whether that journey represents Gaskell's radicalism or its limits is exactly the question we'll keep turning over.
After the break, we move into the Thornton household itself — power, paternalism, and the curious tenderness of a man who runs a cotton mill.

segments.title: Form and Feeling: How Gaskell Builds Tension

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the programme that takes Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
Today we're looking at something that makes the novel so distinctively pleasurable to read: the way Gaskell builds tension — romantic, social, moral — out of the most precisely observed details.
Joining me are three extraordinary readers of this novel, each of whom I suspect has strong and rather different views on what Gaskell is actually doing.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears Gaskell the way a musician hears a score, noting every rest and accent.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings decades of Oxford scholarship to bear — he reads Gaskell as a moralist of the first rank, not a social polemicist.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Gaskell as an anatomist of class power — someone who understood the machinery of industrial capitalism better than she perhaps admitted.
Edmund, I want to begin with you, because you've written about that first encounter between Margaret and Thornton as one of the great charged meetings in Victorian fiction.
Yes — and it repays rereading almost more than any other scene in the novel, precisely because the tension is generated with such economy.
Gaskell gives us two people of formidable self-possession encountering each other, and she shows us immediately — and with great delicacy — that only one of them is actually discomfited.
She writes — and one must hear this carefully —

"a young lady of a different type to most of those he was in the habit of seeing. Her dress was very plain: a close straw bonnet of the best material and shape, trimmed with white ribbon; a large Indian shawl, which hung about her in long heavy folds, and which she wore as an empress wears her drapery."
That final image — "as an empress wears her drapery" — is not mere compliment.
It is a precise calibration of Margaret's unconscious authority — she carries herself as someone to whom deference is simply the natural order.
And Thornton — a man of enormous practical power — is simply not equipped for that.
What strikes me every single time I read that passage aloud is the rhythm of the last clause: "which she wore as an empress wears her drapery."
There's an almost stately cadence to it — the repeated "wears," the long vowels in "empress" and "drapery" — Gaskell is writing for the voice.
A lesser novelist would have simply said Margaret looked queenly and moved on.
Gaskell makes you feel the shawl — the weight of it, the way it moves.
And then there's that marvellous detail: he had imagined the daughter was a little girl.
The comedy of that landed expectation — and what bursts through it — is quintessential Gaskell.
I think both of you are right about the craft, but I want to push on what that image of the empress is actually doing in ideological terms.
Margaret's poise is not simply a personal quality — it is the product of a specific class formation, a Southern gentility that reads physical ease as moral superiority.
Thornton's discomfiture is the discomfiture of the self-made man before an inherited code he has not been given access to.
Gaskell sees this clearly — "his being there was of no concern to the beautiful countenance" — that blankness is not indifference, it is the unconscious performance of class privilege.
I would not deny the class dimension, but I think that reading risks flattening what Gaskell is doing morally.
The novel's great project is precisely to test and revise those inherited codes — and it is Thornton, the manufacturer, who is ultimately vindicated by his character.
One thinks of that extraordinary scene in chapter thirty-eight, where Thornton refuses to employ Higgins — and the refusal is itself a form of moral integrity.
He tells Higgins precisely what the Union would say of any other man who undercut wages to save himself —

"You'd be taking less wages than the other labourers — all for the sake of another man's children. Think how you'd abuse any poor fellow who was willing to take what he could get to keep his own children. You and your Union would soon be down upon him."
There is no sentimentality there — only a hard and honest reckoning with the logic Higgins himself has championed.
But Edmund, notice what Gaskell is doing structurally in that exchange.
Thornton's argument is formally correct — and Gaskell gives him some of her sharpest prose to make it.
But the underlying reality is that Higgins is a man who has watched children starve, and he is here asking for work.
The Union logic that Thornton throws back at him is also the system that produced this moment of desperation in the first place.
What I find remarkable is that Gaskell doesn't let Thornton off the hook — even when she gives him the best argument in the room.
When I read that scene aloud, I always feel the sheer velocity of Thornton's speech — the way "No! no!" comes twice, almost impatiently.
He is a man who thinks quickly, speaks quickly, and is genuinely uncomfortable being asked to feel something he has not yet rationalised.
"Let me pass" — three words, and you hear a man who needs to get away from a situation that is beginning to cost him something.
Gaskell writes exits beautifully — she always knows when a character has said more than they intended.

That question of what characters reveal despite themselves takes us to what I think is one of the most quietly devastating passages in the novel — Margaret in chapter forty-six, not grieving lost love, but lost regard.
Edmund, you've written about this passage as the emotional heart of the novel's second movement — would you take us through it?
What Gaskell achieves in this passage is a moral distinction of the finest precision.
Margaret does not grieve that Thornton no longer loves her — she has, as Gaskell tells us, resolutely set that aside.
What she cannot bear is that she has lost his good opinion — his respect — and she reaches for Gerald Griffin's lines to name what she wants.

"but in the respect and high regard which she had hoped would have ever made him willing, in the spirit of Gerald Griffin's beautiful lines, 'To turn and look back when thou hearest / The sound of my name.'"
To be remembered with warmth — not with passion, but with regard — that is what Margaret asks of the man she respects most.
It is one of the most restrained expressions of longing in Victorian literature.
I find it almost unbearable to read aloud, and I mean that as the highest compliment I can give a piece of prose.
The Griffin lines are not decorative — Gaskell deploys them as the only language adequate to a feeling that Margaret herself cannot quite articulate in her own voice.
And the phrase "beautiful lines" — that's Margaret's judgment, not Gaskell's — it tells us Margaret has lived with those lines, has felt their force before this moment.
The whole passage is layered — the narrator, the character, and the borrowed poem all occupying the same sentence simultaneously.
What strikes me is the word "reinstate." Gaskell writes that no explanation could ever reinstate her — not in his love, but in his respect.
That word comes from the vocabulary of position and status — to be reinstated is to be restored to a place you once held.
Even here, in the most intimate register of the novel, Gaskell cannot escape the social architecture of standing and estimation.
Margaret's anguish is emotional and genuine — but it is also mediated by a world in which a woman's worth is always partly in how she is seen.
And of course all of that longing, all of that carefully preserved dignity, resolves in a scene of extraordinary — and extraordinarily quiet — physical tenderness in chapter fifty-two.
Oliver, I suspect that scene has given you something to work with as a performer.
It is the most carefully engineered moment of release in the novel — and Gaskell engineers it in almost complete silence.
The prose strips down to almost nothing at the exact moment of greatest emotion.
"He clasped her close. But they both kept silence."
Six words, a full stop, and then five more.
Gaskell knows — as all great novelists know — that the most powerful moments in fiction are the ones where language steps aside and lets the thing breathe.
And the callback — her hands placed as they once shielded him from the mob — that is years of narrative paying off in a single gesture.
What Gaskell has been building across the entire novel is a vision of character tested to its limit and found — on both sides — to be genuine.
The clasping — the silence — these are not mere romantic convention.
They are the physical expression of two wills that have each bent, each learned, each surrendered something of their pride in order to reach this point.
The novel earns its ending because it has made us feel the cost of every step toward it.
I want to mark something that often gets absorbed into the romance — Margaret's words immediately following that silence: she murmurs her unworthiness.
And Thornton gently repositions her hands — the hands that once shielded him — back into visibility.
He does not tell her she is wrong — he shows her what her courage looked like from where he stood.
That is, to me, the most radical thing in the scene — a man of immense institutional power learning to read a woman's actions on her own terms, not his.
Three quite different emphases — and yet I notice all three of you arrived at the same final word: something earned.
That may say something important about why North and South continues to hold us — the tension it builds is always in service of a reckoning that feels genuinely paid for.
We'll be back after the break to look more closely at the novel's industrial world — the mill, the workers, and the question of who gets to speak.

segments.title: Closing: The Promise of Understanding Across Divides

utterances.text: We've spent this hour inside the early friction of North and South — the misreadings, the mutual incomprehension, the pride that armours people against one another.
But Gaskell is not writing a novel of permanent estrangement — she's writing a novel about the slow, painful possibility of understanding.
I want to ask each of you: what, in these early chapters, is the promise that keeps us reading?
The promise is kept in the comedy, if you know where to listen for it.
Thornton walks away from his first real encounter with Margaret, and what does Gaskell give us?
He mutters to himself — wounded, rattled, protesting too much.
The man cannot stop thinking about her beauty even while insisting he has stopped thinking about it.
That is not the voice of a man done with a woman — that is the voice of a man thoroughly undone by one.
Oliver is right that the comedy signals something, though I'd frame it rather differently.
What Thornton's muttering reveals is not simply attraction — it is a man discovering that his world-view has a gap in it.
He has arranged everything in Milton around the categories of useful and useless — productive and idle.
And here is someone who fits none of those categories and yet commands his entire attention.
That is the engine of the novel — two incomplete moral frameworks, neither adequate on its own, grinding toward each other.
I want to bring Margaret's side of it into the room, because she is doing something equally interesting.
She has revolted against Thornton's boasting about Milton, his cold contempt for improvident workers.
But she makes a crucial distinction — one that the novel keeps returning to.
She tells her father that when Thornton spoke about his shop-boy past, something changed.
Margaret can see past the ideology to the human formation beneath it.
That, I think, is where the novel places its hope — not in some synthesis of North and South, but in the capacity to recognise the person behind the position.
And Gaskell makes sure that hope is purchased at real cost.
Alongside all this social sparring, we have Margaret watching her mother dissolve in the Milton air.
There is a passage where Margaret enters her mother's room and catches something almost unbearable.
A prayer for endurance — not for rescue, not for escape — simply for the strength to bear what is coming.
Gaskell holds both registers at once: the comedy of Thornton's wounded vanity, and this gothic tenderness of a mother in secret pain.
That double register is, for me, the mark of a novelist of the first rank.
The private suffering and the public comedy are not separate stories — they are two aspects of the same moral education.
Margaret must learn to see other people's invisible pain — her mother's, eventually Thornton's, eventually the workers'.
And she begins that education not in any grand confrontation, but in a darkened bedroom, stealing away before her mother hears her.
What strikes me is that the conditions making Mrs. Hale's suffering possible are precisely the conditions Thornton defends.
The Milton air — its depletion, its weight — is not incidental atmosphere.
It is the industrial economy made breathable — or rather, unbreathable — for those it doesn't serve.
The novel asks us to hold that thought at the same time as we warm to Thornton's personal integrity.
That is the genuine difficulty Gaskell sets — and she does not resolve it cheaply.
And perhaps that is the finest compliment we can pay her — that she doesn't let any of us off the hook.
Not Margaret, not Thornton, not the reader.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through these opening chapters with you.
North and South rewards exactly this kind of slow, attentive reading — and we've barely scratched the surface.
Thank you for listening to North and South Unpacked.

c46:p68.text:
They were both of them tired, and Margaret herself so much so, that she
was unwilling to go out as she had proposed to do, and have another
ramble among the woods and fields so close to the home of her childhood.
And, somehow, this visit to Helstone had not been all—had not been
exactly what she had expected. There was change everywhere; slight, yet
pervading all. Households were changed by absence, or death, or
marriage, or the natural mutations brought by days and months and
years, which carry us on imperceptibly from childhood to youth, and
thence through manhood to age, whence we drop like fruit, fully ripe,
into the quiet mother earth. Places were changed—a tree gone here, a
bough there, bringing in a long ray of light where no light was
before—a road was trimmed and narrowed, and the green straggling
pathway by its side enclosed and cultivated. A great improvement it was
called; but Margaret sighed over the old picturesqueness, the old gloom,
and the grassy way-side of former days. She sate by the window on the
little settle, sadly gazing out upon the gathering shades of night,
which harmonized well with her pensive thought. Mr. Bell slept soundly,
after his unusual exercise through the day. At last he was roused by the
entrance of the tea-tray, brought in by a flushed-looking country-girl,
who had evidently been finding some variety from her usual occupation of
waiter, in assisting this day in the hay-field.
c46:p68.summary: Exhausted, Margaret reflects on the pervasive changes at Helstone—trees altered, roads modified, households transformed by absence or death. She meditates on time's inevitable passage from childhood through adulthood to death, while sitting by the window in melancholic contemplation as Mr. Bell sleeps.

“You are unjust,” said Margaret, gently. “Mr. Lennox has only spoken of
the great probability which he believes there to be of your
redeeming—your more than redeeming what you have lost—don’t speak till
I have ended—pray don’t.” And collecting herself once more, she went on
rapidly turning over some law papers, and statement of accounts in a
trembling hurried manner. “Oh! here it is! and—he drew me out a
proposal—I wish he was here to explain it—showing that if you would
take some money of mine, eighteen hundred and fifty-seven pounds, lying
just at this moment unused in the bank, and bringing me in only two and
a half per cent.—you could pay me much better interest, and might go on
working Marlborough Mills.” Her voice had cleared itself and become more
steady. Mr. Thornton did not speak, and she went on looking for some
paper on which were written down the proposals for security; for she was
most anxious to have it all looked upon in the light of a mere business
arrangement, in which the principal advantage would be on her side.
While she sought for this paper, her very heart-pulse was arrested by
the tone in which Mr. Thornton spoke. His voice was hoarse, and
trembling with tender passion, as he said:—
c52:p24.summary: Margaret defends Lennox's optimism, then proposes that Thornton borrow £1,857 of her savings to continue operating his mill; she frames it as a business arrangement advantageous to herself. c10:p3.text:
Mr. Thornton and Mr. Hale were both absorbed in the continuation of some
object which had been started at their last meeting. Margaret was
recalled to a sense of the present by some trivial, low-spoken remark of
her mother’s; and on suddenly looking up from her work, her eye was
caught by the difference of outward appearance between her father and
Mr. Thornton, as betokening such distinctly opposite natures. Her father
was of slight figure, which made him appear taller than he really was,
when not contrasted, as at this time, with the tall, massive frame of
another. The lines in her father’s face were soft and waving, with a
frequent undulating kind of trembling movement passing over them,
showing every fluctuating emotion; the eyelids were large and arched,
giving to the eyes a peculiar languid beauty which was almost feminine.
The brows were finely arched, but were by the very size of the dreamy
lids, raised to a considerable distance from the eyes. Now, in Mr.
Thornton’s face the straight brows fell low over the clear, deep-set,
earnest eyes, which without being unpleasantly sharp, seemed intent
enough to penetrate into the very heart and core of what he was looking
at. The lines in the face were few but firm, as if they were carved in
marble, and lay principally about the lips, which were slightly
compressed, over a set of teeth so faultless and beautiful as to give
the effect of sudden sunlight when the rare bright smile, coming in an
instant and shining out of the eyes, changed the whole look from the
severe and resolved expression of a man ready to do and dare everything,
to the keen, honest, enjoyment of the moment, which is seldom shown so
fearlessly and instantaneously except by children. Margaret liked this
smile; it was the first thing she had admired in this new friend of her
father’s; and the opposition of character, shown in all these details
of appearance she had just been noticing, seemed to explain the
attraction they evidently felt towards each other.
c10:p3.summary: Margaret observes the striking physical contrast between her gentle father and the robust, intense Mr. Thornton, noting how their appearances reflect opposite temperaments and understanding their mutual attraction.
c10:p3.best_quote: The straight brows fell low over the clear, deep-set, earnest eyes, which without being unpleasantly sharp, seemed intent enough to penetrate into the very heart and core of what he was looking at.

It appeared to Mr. Thornton that all these graceful cares were habitual
to the family; and especially of a piece with Margaret. She stood by the
tea-table in a light-coloured muslin gown, which had a good deal of pink
about it. She looked as if she was not attending to the conversation,
but solely busy with the tea-cups, among which her round ivory hands
moved with pretty, noiseless, daintiness. She had a bracelet on one
taper arm, which would fall down over her round wrist. Mr. Thornton
watched the replacing of this troublesome ornament with far more
attention than he listened to her father. It seemed as if it fascinated
him to see her push it up impatiently until it tightened her soft flesh;
and then to mark the loosening—the fall. He could almost have
exclaimed—“There it goes again!” There was so little left to be done
after he arrived at the preparation for tea, that he was almost sorry
the obligation of eating and drinking came so soon to prevent him
watching Margaret. She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of
an unwilling slave; but her eye caught the moment when he was ready for
another cup; and he almost longed to ask her to do for him what he saw
her compelled to do for her father, who took her little finger and thumb
in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues. Mr.
Thornton saw her beautiful eyes lifted to her father, full of light,
half-laughter, and half-love, as this bit of pantomime went on between
the two, unobserved as they fancied, by any. Margaret’s head still
ached, as the paleness of her complexion, and her silence might have
testified; but she was resolved to throw herself into the breach, if
there was any long untoward pause, rather than that her father’s friend,
pupil, and guest should have cause to think himself in any way
neglected. But the conversation went on; and Margaret drew into a
corner, near her mother, with her work, after the tea-things were taken
away; and felt that she might let her thoughts roam, without fear of
being suddenly wanted to fill up a gap.
c10:p2.summary: Thornton watches Margaret serve tea with fascination, noting her grace and composure, while she strives to fulfil her duty as hostess despite a headache and her initial coldness toward him.
c10:p2.best_quote: She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of an unwilling slave; but her eye caught the moment when he was ready for another cup; and he almost longed to ask her to do for him what he saw her compelled to do for her father, who took her little finger and thumb in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues.

c10:p10.text:
“You are mistaken,” said Margaret, roused by the aspersion on her
beloved South to a fond vehemence of defence, that brought the colour
into her cheeks and the angry tears into her eyes. “You do not know
anything about the South. If there is less adventure or less progress—I
suppose I must not say less excitement—from the gambling spirit of
trade, which seems requisite to force out these wonderful inventions,
there is less suffering also. I see men here going about in the streets
who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care—who are not only
sufferers but haters. Now, in the South we have our poor, but there is
not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of
injustice which I see here. You do not know the South, Mr. Thornton,”
she concluded, collapsing into a determined silence, and angry with
herself for having said so much.
c10:p10.summary: Margaret, roused to passionate defence of her beloved South, challenges Thornton's assertions and describes the visible suffering and injustice she observes in Northern factory workers, contrasting it with Southern poverty.

I see men here going about in the streets who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care—who are not only sufferers but haters. Now, in the South we have our poor, but there is not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of injustice which I see here.
